claim: Cáceres's old town was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 (criteria iii, iv) for its intact blend of Roman, Moorish, Gothic and Renaissance architecture, including about thirty towers from the Islamic period.
quote: blend of Roman, Moorish, Gothic, and Renaissance architecture with thirty towers from the Islamic period

claim: The 12th-century Torre de Bujaco, built on reused Roman ashlars and the emblem of Cáceres, is climbable for panoramic views over Plaza Mayor; open Tue-Sun 10:00-14:00 plus afternoons (16:30-19:30 winter / 17:30-20:30 summer), €2.50.
quote: From Tuesday to Sunday: 10:00-14:00 and 16:30-19:30 h. (winter) 10:00-14:00 and 17:30-20:30 h. (summer) ... Cost: €2.50

claim: The Bujaco Tower ticket forms part of the Bujaco heritage/archaeological complex and the same entry also covers the Arco de la Estrella, a wall section, the Tower of the Pulpits and the Torre del Horno; San Francisco Javier's tower is climbable for about €1.50 cash.
quote: With the entrance to the Bujaco Tower, you can also go to the Arco de la Estrella, part of the wall, the Tower of the Pulpits and the Torre del Horno.

claim: The Concatedral de Santa María, built 13th-16th centuries in Romanesque-Gothic-Renaissance styles, presides over Plaza de Santa María and its bell tower can be climbed for views.
quote: stunning example of Gothic architecture, featuring a richly decorated interior and a notable altarpiece

claim: The Arco de la Estrella, an 18th-century gateway at the top of the central stairs off Plaza Mayor, is the main entrance into the walled UNESCO old town; Plaza Mayor was the historic social and political centre, now lined with porticoed bars and restaurants.
quote: The beautiful Arco de la Estrella at the top of the central stairs serves as the gateway to the Old Town of Cáceres ... Plaza Mayor was the social and political centre of Cáceres.

claim: The Palacio de los Golfines de Abajo is the largest palace in the Monumental City, occupying nearly twenty former houses, blending Gothic, Renaissance and Plateresque styles; it served as the Golfín family residence for 500 years before reopening as a museum in 2015.
quote: It is the largest palace in the Monumental City, as it occupied the space of almost twenty houses ... uniting different architectural styles: Gothic, Renaissance and Plateresque

claim: The 16th-century Iglesia de San Mateo, built over a former mosque with a Plateresque portal bearing medallions of Saints Peter, Paul and Matthew, anchors Plaza de San Mateo in the upper old town.
quote: constructed in the 16th century, possibly over the site of an ancient mosque ... portal stands out with plateresque decoration, featuring medallions of Saint Peter and Saint Paul

claim: The 18th-century Baroque Iglesia de San Francisco Javier with its two white towers dominates Plaza de San Jorge, which holds a statue of Saint George (the city patron) slaying a dragon and hosts cultural events.
quote: a statue of the saint slaying a dragon ... surrounded by notable buildings like the Church of San Francisco Javier ... a venue for cultural events and performances

claim: Beneath the 15th-century Palacio de las Veletas (Museo de Cáceres, built on an Almohad alcazaba) lies the best-preserved Hispano-Muslim aljibe in Spain, a 10th-11th-century cistern with five naves of horseshoe-arched barrel vaults.
quote: the best-preserved Hispano-Muslim aljibe, or cistern, in Spain ... formed by five naves separated by barrel vaults and horseshoe arches

claim: The 15th-century Palacio de las Cigüeñas (Palace of the Storks / Ovando), built on a Muslim fortress, is the only Cáceres mansion to keep its original crenellated 25-metre tower after the Catholic Monarchs ordered noble towers shortened; it now holds a weapons museum.
quote: its majestic 25-meter tower ... It is the only defensive structure in the city that has preserved its original height and crenelated top

claim: The 15th-16th-century Palacio de Toledo-Moctezuma is named for Isabel (Tecuichpo) Moctezuma, daughter of Aztec emperor Moctezuma II, who married conquistador Juan Cano Saavedra; its frescoed rooms depict both European and Aztec worlds and it now houses the Provincial Historical Archive.
quote: The palace takes its name from the Aztec Emperor Moctezuma II ... Both cultures, European and Aztec, are depicted in the frescoes ... houses the Provincial Historical Archive
